subject: Biologi
title: Cells and organ systems
sourceSummary: The parts of the cell and their functions, the difference between plant and animal cells, and how cells build up tissues, organs and organ systems.

questions.prompt: Which part of the cell contains the genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell's activity?
questions.opener: Think about which part acts as the cell's "command centre".
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains DNA and controls which proteins the cell will make. The cell membrane regulates transport in and out, the mitochondrion is responsible for energy production, and the cell wall is only found in plant cells.

questions.prompt: Which part of the cell is often called the cell's "power plant" because it breaks down nutrients and releases energy?
questions.opener: Think about cellular respiration — where in the cell does it happen?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrion carries out cellular respiration and converts the energy in sugar into energy the cell can use. The nucleus controls the cell, the cell wall gives plants structural support, and the cell membrane regulates transport.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
questions.opener: Think about what allows plants to stand upright and carry out photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose that provides structural support, as well as chloroplasts for photosynthesis. The nucleus, cell membrane and mitochondria are found in both cell types.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of the cell membrane?
questions.opener: Think of the cell as a house — what does the outer wall do with the door?
choices: To store the cell's genetic material
To regulate which substances enter and leave the cell
To produce energy for the cell
To give the cell its green colour
questions.explanation: The cell membrane surrounds the cell and selectively lets through substances such as nutrients, oxygen and waste. Storing DNA is the nucleus's job, and energy production takes place in the mitochondria.

questions.prompt: What is a group of cells of the same type, with the same function, sitting together, called?
questions.opener: The next level up from the cell in the body's structure.
questions.explanation: Cells of the same type together form a tissue, e.g. muscle tissue. Several different tissues form an organ, and several organs working together form an organ system.

questions.prompt: Which organ is part of the respiratory system?
questions.opener: Think about where oxygen is taken up in the body.
questions.explanation: The lungs are the central organ of the respiratory system, where oxygen is taken up into the blood and carbon dioxide leaves the body. The stomach belongs to the digestive system and the kidneys to the urinary system.

questions.prompt: Explain how cells build up a human body, from cell to organ system. Use the heart as an example.
questions.opener: There are four levels: cell, tissue, organ, organ system — go through them in order.
questions.answer: Cells of the same type form a tissue (e.g. cardiac muscle tissue), several tissues form an organ (the heart), and the heart works together with the blood vessels in the circulatory system (the organ system) to pump blood around the body.
steps: The cell is the smallest living building block of the body, e.g. a cardiac muscle cell.
Many cardiac muscle cells with the same function sit together and form a tissue — cardiac muscle tissue.
Different tissues (muscle tissue, connective tissue, nerve tissue) together build up the organ that is the heart.
The heart works together with the blood vessels and forms the circulatory system, an organ system that transports oxygen and nutrients around the body.

questions.prompt: What are the cell's most important parts called, and what do they do?
questions.opener: Go through the nucleus, the membrane, the mitochondrion and (for plants) the cell wall.
questions.answer: Nucleus: contains DNA/the genetic material and controls the cell's activity · Cell membrane: surrounds the cell and regulates what is transported in and out · Cytoplasm: the gel-like fluid where the cell's parts sit and reactions take place · Mitochondria: carry out cellular respiration, break down sugar and release energy · Cell wall: found only in plant cells, provides structural support and protection, built from cellulose · Chloroplasts: found only in plant cells, carry out photosynthesis · Vacuole: stores water and substances, often large in plant cells.

questions.prompt: What is the gel-like fluid inside the cell called, where the cell organelles are found?
questions.opener: Everything inside the cell, outside the nucleus, is surrounded by this fluid.
questions.explanation: The cytoplasm is the gel-like fluid where the organelles, such as mitochondria, float and where many of the cell's reactions take place.

questions.prompt: Which cell organelle carries out photosynthesis and is found only in plant cells?
questions.explanation: The chloroplast contains chlorophyll and carries out photosynthesis, converting carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen with the help of sunlight. Mitochondria are found in both cell types.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the vacuole, which is often large in plant cells?
questions.opener: Think about what keeps a plant cell firm and rigid.
choices: Stores water and substances, and gives the cell supporting pressure
questions.explanation: The vacuole stores water and other substances. In plant cells it's often large and creates internal pressure (turgor) that keeps the cell firm and rigid — which is why plants wilt when they get too little water.

questions.prompt: Which organ system is responsible for breaking down food and absorbing nutrients?
questions.opener: Think about the path food takes through the body.
questions.explanation: The digestive system, with organs like the mouth, stomach and intestines, breaks down food and absorbs nutrients into the blood.

questions.prompt: What do several different organs working together to perform a shared task in the body get called?
questions.opener: The next level up from organs in the body's structure.
questions.explanation: An organ system consists of several organs working together, such as the heart and blood vessels in the circulatory system. A tissue is a simpler level, made up of cells of the same type.

questions.prompt: Explain how cells build up a human body, from cell to organ system. Use the lung as your example.
questions.opener: The same four levels as in the heart example — go through them in order, but for the lung.
questions.answer: Cells of the same type (e.g. epithelial cells in the airways) form tissue, several tissues form the organ (the lung), and the lung works together with the airways and chest muscles in the respiratory system to take up oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
steps: The cell is the smallest building block, e.g. an epithelial cell in the wall of an air sac.
Many cells with the same job form a tissue, such as the thin tissue lining the air sacs.
Different tissues (epithelial tissue, connective tissue, muscle tissue in the airways) together build up the organ - the lung.
The lung works together with the windpipe, airways and chest muscles to form the respiratory system, an organ system that supplies the body with oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Which part of the cell gives plant cells their structural support and protection, and is built from cellulose?
questions.opener: What makes a plant cell hold a firmer shape than an animal cell?
questions.explanation: The cell wall, built from cellulose, sits outside the cell membrane in plant cells and provides structural support and protection. Animal cells lack a cell wall, which is why they have a rounder, more flexible surface.
